analogy.p: Imagine a crowd of people all looking at a floodlight (the magnet). Each person turns to face it, just as every tiny compass needle turns to line up with the field. Near the floodlight the light is intense and everyone turns sharply and the crowd is packed (strong field, close lines); far away people barely feel it (weak field, spread-out lines). It breaks down because a floodlight is a single source, whereas a magnet has two poles, and magnetic field lines form closed loops from N to S.
analogy.t: Pocket compasses at a football match

bullets: Describe the **poles** of a magnet as the places where the **magnetic forces are strongest**.
State that **like poles repel** and **unlike poles attract**, and that these are **non-contact forces**.
Describe the difference between a **permanent magnet** and an **induced magnet**.
Define a **magnetic field** as the region around a magnet where a force acts on another magnet or on a magnetic material.
Draw and interpret **magnetic field lines**, including their direction and what spacing shows.
Describe how to **plot a magnetic field using a compass**, and explain how a compass shows the Earth has a magnetic field.
core.h: What the specification asks you to know
core.p: This spec point (AQA 4.7.1) is about the **poles of a magnet**, the **forces between magnets**, the difference between **permanent and induced magnets**, and the idea of a **magnetic field** that you can map with field lines or a plotting compass. You must also know that the **Earth has its own magnetic field**, which is why a compass works. It is the foundation for everything else in magnetism (electromagnets, the motor effect, generators and transformers), so the vocabulary you learn here is used again and again.

bullets: The **north-seeking pole** is the end that points towards the Earth's geographic north when the magnet can swing freely; it is usually just called the north pole.
The poles are where the **field is strongest**, so the force on a magnetic object is largest there.
In the middle of a bar magnet the force is much weaker, which is why filings cluster at the ends.
Cutting a magnet in half gives **two complete magnets**, each with a north and a south pole.
Magnets can be **bar magnets**, horseshoe magnets, disc magnets or ring magnets, but all have two poles.
A pole is a place on the magnet; it is not a separate particle or charge, unlike positive and negative electric charges which can exist on their own.
core.p: Every magnet has two **poles**, a **north-seeking pole (N)** and a **south-seeking pole (S)**. The poles are the regions at the ends of a bar magnet where the **magnetic forces are strongest**; you can see this because paper clips or iron filings cluster most thickly at the ends and hardly at all in the middle. The two poles of one magnet can never be separated: if you cut a bar magnet in half you get two smaller magnets, each with its own N and S pole, not a lone north and a lone south.

bullets: **Like poles repel; unlike poles attract** is the rule you must quote exactly.
These are **non-contact forces**, in the same family as gravitational and electrostatic forces.
The force gets **stronger as the magnets get closer** and weaker as they are moved apart.
The two forces form a **Newton's third law pair**: equal in size, opposite in direction, acting on different objects.
If a freely suspended bar magnet turns round to face another magnet's opposite pole, it is because of the turning effect of these forces.
Link to electrostatics: like charges repel and unlike charges attract, but magnetic poles always come in pairs.
core.h: Forces between magnets: attraction and repulsion
core.p: When two magnets are brought close together they exert forces on each other. **Like poles repel** (N and N, or S and S) and **unlike poles attract** (N and S). These are **non-contact forces**, because the magnets push or pull on each other **without touching**, through their magnetic fields. By Newton's third law, the force on magnet A caused by magnet B is **equal and opposite** to the force on B caused by A, even if one magnet is much bigger or stronger than the other.

bullets: Magnetic materials include **iron, steel, cobalt and nickel**; non-magnetic examples include copper, aluminium, brass, plastic, wood.
Steel (an alloy of iron) is magnetic, but **stainless steel** varies, so exam questions normally stick to plain iron or steel.
A magnet can **pick up** a magnetic material (a nail, paper clip, iron filings) but not a non-magnetic one.
Being magnetic is **not** the same as being a magnet: an unmagnetised iron nail is a magnetic material but not a magnet.
The attraction between a magnet and an unmagnetised magnetic material happens because the material becomes an **induced magnet** (next section).
Reasoning test: if an object is **repelled** by a magnet, it must itself be a magnet; attraction alone does not prove it is a magnet.
core.p: Only a few materials are **magnetic**, meaning they are attracted by a magnet and can be made into magnets. The common ones are **iron, steel, cobalt and nickel** (and alloys containing them). Most other materials, such as copper, aluminium, plastic, wood and glass, are **not** attracted to a magnet at all. The force between a magnet and a magnetic material is **always attraction**, never repulsion.

bullets: **Permanent magnet:** has its own field; can attract **or repel** another magnet.
**Induced magnet:** a magnetic material (for example an iron nail) that behaves as a magnet only while in a magnetic field.
**Induced magnetism always causes attraction**, because the pole induced nearest the magnet is the **opposite** of the magnet's pole facing it.
Take the magnet away and the induced magnet **loses most/all of its magnetism**: the paper clips hanging from the nail fall off.
This explains why an unmagnetised iron nail is attracted to **either** pole of a bar magnet.
The only sure test for a permanent magnet is **repulsion**: only a magnet can repel another magnet.
Link to electromagnets: soft iron cores are used because they become strongly induced magnets and lose the magnetism when the current is switched off.
core.p: A **permanent magnet** produces its **own magnetic field** all the time, and it keeps its magnetism even when nothing else is nearby. An **induced magnet** is a material that **becomes a magnet only when it is placed in a magnetic field**. When it is removed from that field it **loses most or all of its magnetism quickly**. Induced magnets are always **attracted** to the magnet that induces them, because the end nearest the magnet becomes the opposite pole.

bullets: Magnetic field: the region where a magnet or magnetic material **experiences a force**.
The force on a magnetic material in a field is always **attraction**; on a magnet it may be attraction or repulsion.
Field strength **decreases with distance** from the magnet; it is greatest at the **poles**.
The field exists in three dimensions around the magnet, even though diagrams are 2D.
A stronger magnet has a stronger field, so it attracts objects from further away.
Quantitative link (later in the course): field strength is measured as magnetic flux density B in tesla (T), used in F = BIl.
core.p: A **magnetic field** is the **region around a magnet where a force acts on another magnet or on a magnetic material** (iron, steel, cobalt, nickel). You cannot see a field, but you can show it with iron filings or a plotting compass. The **strength** of the field depends on the **distance from the magnet**: it is **strongest at the poles** and gets weaker as you move further away. A magnet placed in a strong part of the field feels a larger force than one placed in a weak part.

bullets: Draw field lines with **arrows pointing from N to S** outside the magnet.
**Close lines = strong field** (near the poles); **widely spaced lines = weak field** (far from the magnet).
Field lines **never cross**, because the field at any point has only one direction.
Lines should be **smooth curves** that start and end on the magnet's poles, not on each other.
The direction is defined by what a **north pole** would do: a north pole is pushed away from N and pulled towards S.
Lines are only a model: the field exists in the spaces between lines as well.
Inside the magnet itself the field lines continue from S back to N, forming complete loops (not normally asked at GCSE).
core.p: We draw a magnetic field using **field lines**. The **direction of the field at any point** is the direction of the **force that would act on a north pole placed at that point**. So field lines always run **from the north (seeking) pole to the south (seeking) pole** outside the magnet. The **closer together** the lines are, the **stronger** the field; where they are far apart the field is weak.

bullets: **Bar magnet:** looping lines from N to S, densest at the poles, with arrows on every line.
**Uniform field:** produced between **two opposite poles** placed close together; lines are **straight, parallel and equally spaced**.
**Unlike poles facing (attract):** lines run directly from the N pole to the S pole.
**Like poles facing (repel):** lines bend away from each other and do not join; there is a point between the poles where the field is zero.
At the **edges** of a uniform field the lines bulge outwards and the field weakens.
Always add **at least 3 lines on each side**, symmetrical, with arrows, to earn the drawing marks.
core.h: The field patterns you must be able to draw
core.p: For a **bar magnet** the lines leave the north pole, curve round, and enter the south pole, packed closest at the poles. Between **two unlike poles** facing each other, the lines run straight from the N pole across the gap to the S pole, so the field is **uniform** (parallel, equally spaced lines, constant strength) in the middle of the gap. Between **two like poles** facing each other, the lines bend away and meet in a neutral point where the fields cancel. Exam questions often give an incomplete pattern and ask you to add lines and arrows.

bullets: Place the bar magnet on a sheet of paper and **draw round it**.
Place the compass near one pole and mark with pencil dots **at both ends of the needle**.
Move the compass so that the **tail of the needle is on the previous dot**, then mark the new position of the needle's head.
Repeat until you reach the other pole, then **join the dots** with a smooth line and add an arrow in the direction the **north end of the needle** points.
Start at different places around the magnet to build up a **pattern of lines**.
Alternative: sprinkle **iron filings** on paper over a magnet and tap gently; they become induced magnets and line up along the field, but this does not show direction.
Accuracy tip: keep other magnets and iron objects well away, because they distort the field and the compass readings.
core.h: Plotting a magnetic field with a compass (method)
core.p: A **plotting compass** contains a small **bar magnet** (the needle) that is free to turn. Its needle lines up with the magnetic field at its position, with the north-seeking end showing the **direction of the field**. By moving the compass step by step you can trace out a complete field line. This method is the one examiners expect you to describe in 4 mark questions, so learn the order of the steps.

bullets: The compass needle is a **magnet that aligns itself with the Earth's field** and points north.
The fact that a compass points north shows that the **Earth's core is magnetic** (made largely of iron and nickel).
The Earth's field is like a **huge bar magnet** tilted slightly from its rotation axis.
Near the geographic north the Earth behaves like a magnetic **south** pole; that is why the north-seeking pole of a compass points there.
Near a magnet or a current-carrying wire the compass instead points along the local, stronger field, which is how it can detect fields.
Compasses are used for navigation; they are only reliable away from magnets, steel structures and electric currents.
core.h: The Earth's magnetic field and the compass
core.p: A **magnetic compass** contains a small bar magnet that points in the direction of the **Earth's magnetic field**, which is why a freely turning compass needle always settles pointing roughly **north**. This shows that the **Earth has a magnetic field**, and so the **Earth's core must be magnetic**. The Earth's field is similar in shape to that of a **bar magnet**, with field lines running from the south of the planet towards the north. Because opposite poles attract, the compass needle's north-seeking pole is attracted to a magnetic **south** pole near the geographic north.

bullets: **Fields of wires and solenoids (4.7.2):** the same field-line rules (N to S, closer = stronger, never cross) apply.
**Motor effect (4.7.2/4.7.3):** a wire in a magnetic field feels a force because the two fields interact.
**Generator effect:** a changing magnetic field induces a potential difference; the strength of the field matters.
**Transformers:** use an iron core that is repeatedly magnetised and demagnetised, so it must be a material that is easily induced.
**Forces topic:** magnetic force is a non-contact force alongside gravitational and electrostatic.
**Space and Earth:** the Earth's magnetic field and compass links to geography of navigation.
core.p: The ideas of poles, fields and induced magnetism come back in later topics. The field around a **current-carrying wire** has the same properties as a magnet's field and can be mapped with the same plotting compass (4.7.2). The **motor effect** depends on the interaction of two magnetic fields, and **generators and transformers** rely on changing magnetic fields. Understanding why iron cores become induced magnets also explains why they make electromagnets so much stronger.

bullets: **Find the poles:** arrows pointing **away** from a pole means **north**; pointing **into** a pole means **south**.
**Compare strengths:** the point where field lines are **closest together** has the strongest field.
**Predict a compass:** the north end of a compass needle points in the same direction as the field line at that point.
**Spot a neutral point:** where two fields cancel, there are no lines and a compass shows no preferred direction.
**Attract or repel?** Lines joining two magnets directly means attract; lines bending away means repel.
In data tables of paper clips picked up at different distances, say that strength **decreases as distance increases** and quote values.
core.p: Many marks come from reading diagrams. When shown a field pattern, look at the **line spacing** to compare strengths and at the **arrows** to find poles: arrows leave a north pole and enter a south pole. If a diagram shows lines bending towards each other between two magnets, the poles are unlike; if they curve away, the poles are like. Compass questions are answered by recalling that the needle's north end points along the field line direction.

bullets: Explain **induced attraction**: nearest induced pole is opposite to the magnet's pole, so attraction results for either pole.
Explain **why steel keeps magnetism longer than soft iron**: steel is magnetically hard (used for permanent magnets); soft iron is magnetically soft (used in electromagnets).
Explain **why a compass can detect a current**: the current's field is stronger than the Earth's locally, so the needle turns.
Explain **why field lines never cross**: a crossing point would mean two directions of force at one point.
Use the **exact definition**: 'region around a magnet where a force acts on another magnet or magnetic material'.
Always state direction as **'from north to south'** and mention the arrow.
Link force to **distance** whenever asked to compare positions.
core.p: There is no separate Higher-only content in this spec point, but top-grade answers use precise explanations of **why** things happen. For example, an induced magnet is attracted because the pole induced nearest to the magnet is always opposite, so the force is attractive whichever pole of the real magnet is used. A good explanation of the compass also mentions that the Earth's magnetic south pole is near the geographic north pole.

exam: **Command words:** 'state' needs a short fact (like poles repel); 'describe' needs a clear sequence; 'explain' needs a reason linked with 'because'.
**1-mark:** give the rule 'like poles repel, unlike poles attract' or name a magnetic material (iron, steel, cobalt, nickel).
**2-mark definitions:** magnetic field = region where a force acts on a magnet or magnetic material (two ideas: region + force).
**Induced magnet explanation (3 marks):** it becomes a magnet when in a magnetic field; the nearest pole is opposite; so it is attracted.
**Plotting a field (4 marks):** draw round magnet, compass near pole, mark both ends of needle, move compass to the dot, join dots, add arrow N to S.
**Drawing field lines:** use smooth curves (not straight lines), arrows from N to S, lines closer at poles, never crossing; add at least 3 lines each side.
**Comparing strength:** say 'the field lines are closer together at X so the field is stronger at X'.
**Compass and Earth:** say 'the needle points north because the Earth has a magnetic field; its core must be magnetic'.
**Uniform field:** 'parallel, equally spaced lines, between two opposite poles'.
**Link data skills:** if given distance vs force data, state that force decreases with distance and use numbers.

mistakes.r: Only magnetic materials (iron, steel, cobalt, nickel) are attracted; copper and aluminium are not.
Field lines go from north to south outside the magnet.
mistakes.w: Field lines go from south to north.

mistakes.r: A magnetic material is only ever attracted; repulsion shows both objects are magnets.
mistakes.w: Repulsion can happen between a magnet and an iron nail.

mistakes.r: It loses most or all of its magnetism quickly when removed from the field.
mistakes.w: An induced magnet keeps its magnetism.

mistakes.r: Field lines never cross because the field has one direction at each point.
mistakes.w: Field lines can cross when two magnets are close.

mistakes.r: The poles are the ends, where the forces are strongest.
mistakes.w: The poles are in the centre of the magnet.

mistakes.r: The compass's north-seeking pole is attracted to a magnetic south pole near geographic north.
mistakes.w: The compass points to the geographic north because it is a north pole there.

mistakes.r: It is a non-contact force acting through the field.
mistakes.w: Magnetic force is a contact force.

summary: You must know that magnets have poles where the force is strongest, that like poles repel and unlike attract, how permanent and induced magnets differ, and how a magnetic field is shown by field lines and mapped with a compass (including the Earth's field). It matters because every later magnetism topic (electromagnets, motors, generators, transformers) builds on these ideas.

terms.d: The place on a magnet where the magnetic forces are strongest.
The end of a magnet that points towards the Earth's geographic north when free to turn.
A force that acts between objects without them touching, such as the force between magnets.
A magnet that produces its own magnetic field.
A material that becomes a magnet when placed in a magnetic field and loses most or all of its magnetism when removed.
A material, such as iron, steel, cobalt or nickel, that is attracted by a magnet.
The region around a magnet where a force acts on another magnet or on a magnetic material.
A line showing the direction of the force on a north pole placed at that point; it runs from north to south.
A field with the same strength and direction everywhere, shown by parallel, equally spaced lines.
A small compass containing a bar magnet that lines up with the magnetic field at its position.
A point where two magnetic fields cancel so the resultant field is zero.
Two poles of the same type (N and N or S and S), which repel.
Two poles of different type (N and S), which attract.
The magnetic field around the Earth, produced by its magnetic core, similar to that of a bar magnet.
Tiny iron pieces that become induced magnets and line up along field lines.

worked.ans: Model answer: Draw round the magnet. Place the plotting compass close to one pole and mark both ends of the needle with dots. Move the compass so the tail end of the needle is on the last dot and mark again. Repeat until the other pole is reached, join the dots to make one field line, and mark an arrow from north to south. Repeat from other starting points to build up the pattern.
worked.q: Describe how you would plot the magnetic field of a bar magnet using a plotting compass. (4 marks)
steps: Place the bar magnet on a sheet of paper and draw around it so it can be put back.
Put the plotting compass near the north pole and mark with a pencil dot the two ends of the needle.
Move the compass so that the end of the needle sits on the previous dot, and mark the new position of the other end.
Repeat until you reach the south pole, then join the dots with a smooth line and add an arrow in the direction the north end of the needle pointed.

worked.ans: The nail becomes an induced magnet in the bar magnet's field, with the nearest end an opposite pole to the magnet's pole. Unlike poles attract, so it is attracted to either end.
worked.q: An unmagnetised iron nail is attracted to both ends of a bar magnet. Explain why. (3 marks)
steps: Identify what happens to the nail: the nail is a magnetic material so it becomes an induced magnet in the magnet's field.
State which pole forms: the end nearest the bar magnet's pole becomes the opposite pole.
Link to force: unlike poles attract, so the nail is attracted whichever end of the magnet is used.

worked.ans: X has the stronger field because the lines are closer together; a compass at X points along the field line in the direction of the arrow (north to south).
worked.q: A student draws field lines around two magnets. At point X the lines are 2 mm apart and at point Y they are 9 mm apart. Which point has the stronger field, and how does a compass at X behave? (2 marks)
steps: Compare spacing: closer lines mean a stronger field, so X is stronger.
Compass: the needle lines up with the local field, with the north end pointing along the arrow on the line.
